clue.text: Charles Dickens's old man (rather dim-witted)

parts.note: Boz was the pen name Charles Dickens used for his early sketches

explanation.surface: Someone describes an elderly character from Dickens, adding in brackets that he is a bit slow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charles Dickens's' is not a possessive pointing at one of his characters: it asks for the writer's own pen name, BOZ.
explanation.definitionFit: A bozo is slang, chiefly American, for a foolish or stupid fellow.

clue.text: Pyramid builder's revolutionary works

definitions.note: the 's stands for 'is', so the definition is the pyramid builder himself

parts.note: Che Guevara is the crossword's stock revolutionary
OPS is short for opuses, a composer's works

explanation.surface: The pyramid builder's achievements are described as revolutionary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolutionary' reads as an adjective praising the works, but it is a noun giving CHE.
explanation.definitionFit: The Egyptian pharaoh Khufu, called Cheops by the Greeks, built the Great Pyramid of Giza.

clue.text: Nick's apparently in

definitions.note: the 's stands for 'is'; to nick is to steal

parts.note: the two letters i-n are the first half of the four-letter unit of length, so 'in' is what you get from a half of that word

explanation.surface: A terse remark that someone called Nick has apparently arrived.
explanation.walkthrough: Half of the word INCH is IN, so 'in' is apparently a half inch. Half-inch is Cockney rhyming slang for pinch, i.e. steal.
explanation.definitionFit: In rhyming slang 'half-inch' stands for pinch, which is a slang verb for stealing, just as nick is.

clue.text: After removing cap, clerk appears comparatively grey

indicators.note: a cap is worn on top, so removing it takes away the first letter of the word

parts.note: a cashier is a bank or shop clerk who handles money

explanation.surface: An office clerk takes off his hat and turns out to be greyer than expected.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After removing cap' drops the C at the head of CASHIER.
explanation.definitionFit: Ashy means pale grey like ash, and the comparative form means greyer.

clue.text: It could be a statement about the domestic arrangements when there's no home help?

definitions.text: It could be a statement about the domestic arrangements when there's no home help?

parts.words: It could be a statement about the domestic arrangements when there's no home help
parts.note: with no hired cleaner, mother does the cleaning herself, a remark that splits into a char (cleaning lady), is, and ma (mother); and 'It' is also slang for personal magnetism

explanation.surface: Someone muses on who does the housework when nobody is employed to clean.
explanation.walkthrough: A char is a British charwoman, a cleaner. The answer splits as CHAR IS MA: mother is the cleaner. 'It' in the old sense of sex appeal also points to the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Charisma is personal magnetism, the quality once called simply 'It' in the Clara Bow sense.

clue.text: A pope's exclamation of surprise at these baseless untrue stories?

definitions.text: A pope's exclamation of surprise at these baseless untrue stories?

parts.words: A pope's exclamation of surprise at these baseless untrue stories
parts.note: Urban was the name of several popes and 'My!' is a cry of surprise, so the pope's reaction to such tales comes out as his name plus a word for unfounded stories

explanation.surface: A pontiff gasps at some groundless tall tales.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer splits as URBAN (a papal name, as in Urban II) and MY (an exclamation of surprise), with THS left over to finish the stories.
explanation.definitionFit: Urban myths are widely retold modern tales, such as alligators in sewers, that have no factual basis.

clue.text: Arkwright's evident lack of surprise

definitions.note: the 's stands for 'is'; an arkwright is jokingly a builder of an ark

parts.note: no means none, a lack of something
Ah! is an exclamation of surprise

explanation.surface: Arkwright, the shopkeeper or inventor, shows no surprise at all.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard Arkwright was a textile inventor and Arkwright the shopkeeper of the British sitcom Open All Hours, but here the word is read as an ark-wright, a maker of arks.
explanation.definitionFit: A wright is a maker, so the builder of the biblical ark is jokingly its wright.

clue.text: Mixed metaphors back in the air

indicators.note: metaphors that are mixed are jumbled together, so the letters of that word are rearranged
the back of a word is its end, so this takes the final letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: Clashing figures of speech are returning to the airwaves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mixed' rearranges METAPHORS into ATMOSPHER, and 'back in' takes the E at the end of 'the'.
explanation.definitionFit: The atmosphere is the air surrounding the earth, and also the mood or feel of a place.

clue.text: French writer, male, is dead square? Wrong!

indicators.note: something wrong is out of order, so these letters must be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone protests that calling a French author, male and deceased, old-fashioned is mistaken.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Square' looks like a jibe at a dull man, but it is just fodder: 'Wrong' rearranges IS DEAD SQUARE into ARQUISDESADE.
explanation.definitionFit: The Marquis de Sade was an eighteenth-century French novelist whose name gave us the word sadism.

clue.text: Company device needs two fellows to sign out

parts.note: a logo is the emblem or device a company uses
F is the abbreviation for fellow, so two of them give FF

explanation.surface: A firm's emblem has to be signed off by two senior colleagues.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sign' looks like signing off a design, but 'sign out' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To log off is to end a session on a computer system, signing out of it.

clue.text: Line of force

definitions.meaning: a line is a railway track
to force or rush them into something

explanation.surface: A physics phrase for the direction a force acts along.
explanation.definitionFit: A railway line is an American railroad, and to railroad is to push something through by force.

clue.text: Greek characters in a university city in Europe

parts.note: chi is a letter of the Greek alphabet, and the plural gives CHIS

explanation.surface: Members of Greek-letter societies are at a university somewhere in Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Greek characters' suggests fraternity members, but it just means letters: two chis.
explanation.definitionFit: Chisinau is the capital of Moldova, in eastern Europe.

clue.text: Barge secreting pitch and fuel creates a song and dance

indicators.note: to secrete is to hide away, so the barge holds the other pieces inside it

parts.note: a hoy is a heavy sailing barge
a key is the pitch a piece of music is set in
coke is a fuel made from coal

explanation.surface: A boat smuggling tar and fuel causes a big fuss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a song and dance' reads as a fuss, but literally the hokey-cokey is a song with a dance. A hoy is an old barge.
explanation.definitionFit: The hokey-cokey is a British party song with actions, known as the hokey-pokey elsewhere.

clue.text: Some system users about to restart

indicators.note: about here means turned round, so the run is read backwards
only some of the letters of the following words are used, a run lying inside them

explanation.surface: A few computer users are on the point of rebooting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' takes EMUSER from inside 'system users' and 'about' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: To resume is to begin again after a pause, taking up where one left off.

clue.text: Adventurers of yore and lore? Think G&S, literally

parts.note: the letters t-h-i-n-k-g-s, read literally without the ampersand, wander into a new order to give the medieval title, the second word signalling the shuffle

explanation.surface: A puzzle about old heroes invites us to think of Gilbert and Sullivan.
explanation.walkthrough: G&S (Gilbert and Sullivan) suggests their operettas, but 'literally' means take the letters THINKGS; KNIGHTS is those letters gone astray, so errant (wandering) acts as an anagram indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: Knights errant were wandering medieval knights in search of adventure, in history and in romance.

clue.text: Diana upset royalty, ultimately lacking unbridled adoration

indicators.note: upset means knocked over or out of order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: Di is the short form of Diana

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter, which is missing

explanation.surface: Princess Diana upset the royal family, who lacked any wild devotion to her.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ultimately lacking' drops the last Y of royalty, and 'upset' rearranges DI with ROYALT.
explanation.definitionFit: Idolatry is excessive, uncritical worship of a person or thing.

clue.text: Orderly hoards liquid fuel, sadly

indicators.note: to hoard is to keep something stored inside, so one piece holds the other

parts.note: ruly is the rare positive of unruly, meaning orderly

indicators.note: liquid means fluid, flowing, so the letters of the word flow into a new order

explanation.surface: A tidy-minded person stockpiles liquid fuel, sad to say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'liquid fuel' reads as a phrase, but 'liquid' rearranges FUEL to EFUL, which RULY holds.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruefully means with regret or sorrow, which is close to sadly.

clue.text: Miss March and Victor participated in run? I don't believe it!

indicators.note: the two pieces take part in the run by going inside it

parts.note: in cricket a bye is a run scored without the batsman hitting the ball
Jo March is a heroine of Little Women
Victor is V in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone is amazed that two named people took part in a race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Miss March' looks like failing to march, but it is Jo March of Little Women. A bye is a cricket run scored without a hit.
explanation.definitionFit: By Jove is an old-fashioned exclamation of astonishment or disbelief.

clue.text: Woman from 70s band is on ecstasy

parts.note: ELO, the Electric Light Orchestra, was a hit band of the 1970s
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A woman from a seventies pop group is taking drugs.
explanation.definitionFit: Eloise is a female first name, as in the medieval Heloise.

clue.text: A way to reduce excess baggage duty I'm not sure will be accepted

definitions.text: A way to reduce excess baggage

indicators.note: the hesitation is accepted, taken inside the duty

parts.note: excise is a duty or tax on goods
er is the hesitant sound of someone unsure

explanation.surface: An airline passenger wonders whether paying for extra luggage will be allowed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'excess baggage' suggests airport fees, but it means extra body weight.
explanation.definitionFit: Physical activity burns off surplus weight, the excess baggage around the waist.

clue.text: Nut, for example, punching champ

indicators.note: the piece punches its way into the middle of the other

parts.note: to champ is to chew noisily
as can mean 'for example', as in 'animals as cats'

explanation.surface: A nut, say, is hit by a boxing champion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'champ' looks like a boxing champion, but it is the verb, to chew.
explanation.definitionFit: The cashew is a kidney-shaped nut from a tropical tree.

clue.text: Unenthusiastic about Charlie and Bill having a drink

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece goes round the others

parts.note: cool means lukewarm, unenthusiastic
Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet
AC is short for account, a bill

explanation.surface: Someone is lukewarm about Charlie and Bill going for a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charlie and Bill' look like two drinkers, but give C and AC; COOL goes about them, then A.
explanation.definitionFit: Coca-Cola is the best-known brand of cola soft drink.

clue.text: Insecure US nurse dropping son off

indicators.note: off means wrong or out of place, so the remaining letters are rearranged
dropping means letting go, so that letter is removed

explanation.surface: A nervous American nurse drops her son off somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dropping son off' reads as a school run: 'dropping' removes an S, and 'off' rearranges UNURSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Unsure means lacking confidence, which is what insecure means.

clue.text: Do bridge partners have to be kicked out of unkindness?

indicators.note: kicking out means expelling, so these letters are removed

parts.note: an unkindness is the collective noun for a group of ravens
North and South are partners at bridge, giving N and S

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether partners at the card table must be expelled for being unkind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unkindness' looks like the reason for expulsion, but it is the collective noun for ravens.
explanation.definitionFit: A do is a party, and a rave is a large dance party.

clue.text: Film director gets to know English philosopher

parts.note: ken is an old or Scots verb meaning to know
Bertrand Russell was an English philosopher

explanation.surface: A film director becomes acquainted with an English thinker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gets to know' looks like one phrase, but 'gets' is a link and 'to know' gives KEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Ken Russell was a British director of films such as Women in Love and Tommy.

clue.text: Diplomat without the least trace of original sin

indicators.note: without means lacking, so a letter is taken away

parts.note: an envoy is a diplomatic representative

indicators.note: the least trace of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A diplomat free from any taint of original sin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'original sin' looks like one phrase, but 'original' only gives O, removed from ENVOY.
explanation.definitionFit: Envy is one of the seven deadly sins.
